newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU's Van Miert warns over BA-American linkup.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU's Van Miert warns over BA-American linkup.

text.p: European Union commissioners sent a fresh warning to British Airways and American Airlines on Tuesday that the EU would not close its eyes to their proposed mega-alliance but said a decision would be taken within weeks.
Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock said the commission's final decision on the deal will come within weeks, rather than months.

In a speech made available ahead of delivery, Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert Van Miert repeated earlier statements that the two companies would control 61 percent of the passenger transport between Britain and the United States -- something the Commission could not ignore.

He also stressed to the European Parliament that the Commission needed more information on the alliance, despite having already received written and oral answers from both companies to its objections.
Van Miert did not elaborate on the additional information required.

Kinnock, who shares responsibility with Van Miert for assessing the proposed alliance, told Reuters when asked how long it will take the Commission to reach its decision: "It's not months, it's not far away..."

The Commission's authority to investigate the link-up has been openly challenged by BA and the British government. Both argue the British antitrust authorities have a greater say than the Commission, whose jurisdiction only applies clearly to deals involving EU-based carriers.
But the Commission points out that the deal would affect traffic with mainland Europe, not just Britain.
"The effects of this agreement will be felt in the whole Union, not just Britain," he said.

In a move to avoid future jurisdictional conflicts with national governments, Van Miert announced the Commission would "soon" propose modifying EU air transport legislation to cover services with non-EU countries.
Any changes will have to be approved by EU transport ministers.

The Commission started separate probes in July into several transatlantic air deals but the BA-American link-up is the only one to have attracted headlines because it is the largest and the Commission has publicly said that it raises important competition concerns.

The announcement by Britain's Office of Fair Trading in December that it would clear the alliance on the condition the airlines gave up 168 weekly slots at the congested London Heathrow airport to make room for rivals did everything but assuage such fears.

This is because the companies have said, at least publicly, they would sell the landing and taking off rights, not surrender them. EU legislation only provides for the exchange of slots, as the Commission recalled harshly in a letter to the British Department of Industry in January.

The Commission sent the two airlines a so-called statement of objections in October detailing its concerns. Van Miert said he had received written and oral answers, but was expecting "supplementary information".
The Commission will consult a panel of national experts before reaching a final decision, Van Miert said. He did not say when this would happen.

The alliance also faces a regulatory hurdle in the United States where it has been made conditional to the conclusion of an "open skies" agreement opening up the UK-U.S. aviation market to competing airlines.
